implementerProof.how: Five of the six entries re-verify at this head, driven independently on the tester's own harness (its own mock resource monitor, none of the implementer's driver): the rendering is byte-identical to the head the tester verified in round 1 except for the one added lifecycle block on the app's envoy-dispatch container (entries 1, 2 and the arrangement); the schema and SDK are untouched by this round, since dispatch.go is unchanged (entry 3); the migration rule and its two cited facts still hold (entry 4); and the allowedNamespaces policy now renders and is pinned at two rules, the second the front door's, which the tester re-rendered at the consuming stack's input shape and re-ran as a test (entry 6). Entry 5 is rejected. Its central claim — 'The hook runs before SIGTERM, inside the unchanged 30 s grace, so cmd/dispatch/shutdown.go's own drain budget is untouched' — is false against the Kubernetes contract it depends on, and the thing it claims to prove is the defect recorded in failures[0]. Separately, every one of the six entries records headSha f8ec21dfc7245cd25eec7a9ee24c6b05b1aa0d46, which is not a commit of this repository (failures[1]), so no entry can be checked at the commit it names.

failures.criterion: Deliverable 1 / review round 1 finding 1: the app rolls a new image in without taking Dispatch away, which requires each terminating pod to finish the shutdown envoy-dispatch is written for. The pre-stop wait added this round is taken out of that shutdown rather than added to the pod's budget, so every terminating pod now has five seconds less than its server assumes.
failures.evidence: The app pod renders terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 with lifecycle.preStop.exec.command ['sleep','5'] on envoy-dispatch (tester's own Construct dump at this head: 'example-dispatch: grace=30 lifecycle=envoy-dispatch=sleep 5'; the front door and the listener carry none). The kubelet runs the preStop hook first and sends SIGTERM only after it returns, inside that one grace period — kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle, Pod termination: 'If one of the Pod's containers has defined a preStop hook ... the kubelet runs that hook inside of the container ... If the preStop hook needs longer to complete than the default grace period allows, you must modify terminationGracePeriodSeconds to suit this', and only then 'The kubelet triggers the container runtime to send a TERM signal to process 1'. So envoy-dispatch now has 25 s after SIGTERM, not 30. Its shutdown is built for 30: cmd/dispatch/shutdown.go declares stopGrace = 30 * time.Second as 'how long Dispatch's runtime lets it run after SIGTERM before killing it', and derives documentShutdownTimeout = docs.ShutdownDrainBudget (9 s, internal/dispatch/docs/service.go:597) + 5 s = 14 s and httpDrainBeforeDocuments = 30 - 5 - 14 = 11 s, so the planned sequence ends at 25 s with a five-second reserve that the file says exists to outlast a measured 3.4 s settlement overrun. At 25 s that reserve is exactly zero, and cmd/dispatch/shutdown_test.go's TestSIGTERMWhileAWriteWaitsOnALockCommitsItAndAnswersBeforeExit — a write that commits and answers 27 s after SIGTERM, '3 s inside the runtime's kill' — is SIGKILLed mid-commit on every rolling update, the path this issue delivers. Red test: TestDispatchAppPodGracePeriodCoversThePreStopWaitAndTheServersShutdown in packages/envoy/infra/gcp/dispatch_test.go, committed at 51f3c6a08972; `cd packages/envoy/infra && go test -p 1 -count=1 -run TestDispatchAppPodGracePeriodCoversThePreStopWaitAndTheServersShutdown ./gcp/` fails with '"30" is not greater than or equal to "35"'. The fix is the pod's budget, not the wait: TerminationGracePeriodSeconds 35 (the five-second wait plus the thirty the server assumes). TestDispatchAppPodKeepsServingUntilItsRemovalFromRoutingPropagates pins the 30 and must be updated with it, and the code comment at dispatch_kube.go ('so it takes nothing from the server's own drain budget') and the implement handoff's proof entry 5 say the opposite of the contract and need correcting too; dispatch-pod.golden changes with the field.

unproven: Unchanged from round 1 and still INFRA-63's to settle: no pod in Legion reaches a cluster or the consuming stack's state, so Tailscale Serve resolving the app's cluster DNS name under TS_USERSPACE=true, the cutover's two tailscaled processes against one state Secret (the consuming program still mints the tailnet key Reusable: false), the front door's unmeasured 100m/128Mi reservation, and whether a release loses no request are all unproved here.

The pre-stop wait's five seconds are themselves unmeasured — whether that covers EndpointSlice propagation plus Tailscale Serve's own routing refresh is what the consuming stack's measured release settles. The README says so. Raising the pod's grace period to cover the wait, which failures[0] asks for, is correct whatever that measurement later changes the wait to, since the invariant the red test pins is a relation between the two numbers.
observations: README wording, not a defect: 'a stopping pod keeps serving for five seconds after it is removed from routing' reads as though the wait begins once removal has propagated. The hook and the EndpointSlice update start together, when the pod is marked terminating; the five seconds are the window the propagation has to finish inside. Worth a word when that paragraph is edited for failures[0] anyway.
